questions.question: How would you design a scalable CSS theme for reusable components?
questions.title: Scalable component theming
questions.direct_answer: Define a small set of semantic global tokens, map them to component-level custom properties where needed, and let themes override values at clear DOM boundaries. Keep component structure stable, document the public tokens, and test contrast and states in every theme.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can apply custom properties, scoping, and cascade layers in one maintainable design.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Exposing every internal value globally or duplicating component selectors per theme.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate global semantics, component defaults, and supported override points.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Global tokens describe shared roles such as surface, text, and accent.
Component tokens translate global roles into local decisions.
Theme boundaries override values instead of copying component rules.
Every theme must preserve contrast, focus, hover, and disabled states.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I start with semantic global tokens such as `--color-surface`, `--color-text`, and `--color-accent`. Their names describe purpose rather than a fixed palette, so light, dark, or high-contrast themes can assign different concrete values without changing component CSS.

A reusable component may map those globals to a small public API. A button can define `--button-bg: var(--color-accent)` and use that internally. A product area can override the documented button token without reaching into every private padding, shadow, or nested selector.

For example, `html[data-theme='dark']` replaces the global surface and text tokens. A warning panel locally replaces `--button-bg`, so only actions inside that boundary adopt the warning treatment. Inheritance distributes values through both cases.

I establish cascade layers for foundations and components, avoid global names for temporary internals, and provide literal fallbacks where a component must remain usable on its own. JavaScript owns the selected theme attribute; CSS owns the palette and component presentation.

Scalability includes verification. I test text contrast, visible focus, hover and pressed states, form controls, charts, and images in every supported theme. A token system reduces duplication, but it does not prove that all value combinations remain readable.

sections.title: Build a narrow token contract
sections.content: Global tokens carry site-wide meaning. Component tokens expose deliberate customization points. Private component declarations consume those tokens. This three-level boundary prevents a theme from depending on the component's internal selector structure.

sections.title: Too many tokens can be another form of coupling
sections.content: Turning every margin and border into a public custom property makes the API harder to understand and prevents safe refactoring. Expose values that consumers genuinely need to vary, keep internal calculations private, and document fallback relationships. A component should render a coherent default even when no product theme overrides it.

sections.title: Token ownership from theme to element
sections.content:
theme values
  ↓ override
global semantic tokens (--color-accent)
  ↓ mapped into
component public tokens (--button-bg)
  ↓ consumed by
private button declarations

sections.title: Map a global role into a component token

followup_questions: Which design tokens belong globally and which belong to a component?

questions.question: How would you fix a dropdown that works only on hover?
questions.title: Making a hover dropdown keyboard and touch friendly
questions.direct_answer: Use a real button to control the dropdown, expose its open state with aria-expanded, and toggle the panel with click or keyboard activation. Hover may enhance pointer use, but focus, touch, Escape, outside interaction, and focus return need explicit behaviour.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands the boundary between CSS states and interactive component behaviour.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding :focus to a non-focusable div or relying on :hover for touch and keyboard users.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Define semantic control, state synchronization, dismissal, and focus behaviour.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A dropdown trigger should be a real button.
aria-expanded and the panel's hidden state must stay synchronized.
Click and keyboard activation must work without hover.
Escape, outside dismissal, and focus return need a defined rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A hover-only dropdown assumes a fine pointer and gives the browser no durable open state. I replace the trigger with a real button so Enter, Space, focus, and accessible naming work without recreating button behaviour on a div.

The button carries `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, while the panel uses the `hidden` attribute when closed. One click handler updates both values. CSS can still use hover for a visual preview, but the actual menu remains controlled by an explicit state that works on touch and keyboard.

For example, selecting the Products button opens a panel of ordinary links. Escape closes the panel and returns focus to Products. Clicking outside can close it, but moving the pointer through a small gap does not unexpectedly dismiss a keyboard-open panel.

I do not automatically add ARIA menu roles to normal site navigation. Those roles bring desktop-application keyboard expectations. A disclosure containing links is often the simpler semantic pattern unless the component truly implements a menu widget.

I test Tab order, Enter and Space, Escape, touch input, zoom, and a screen reader. CSS handles layout and visible focus; JavaScript handles the durable open state and dismissal rules that selectors alone cannot reliably coordinate.

sections.title: Hover is an input signal, not application state
sections.content: A pointer temporarily crossing a trigger does not describe whether a panel should remain open for touch or keyboard use. A button-owned boolean state gives every input method the same component, while CSS still styles hover and focus feedback.

sections.title: CSS interaction pattern selection
sections.content: A disclosure button plus a region or navigation list is sufficient for many website dropdowns. A true ARIA menu requires arrow-key movement, menuitem roles, focus management, and a behaviour model users expect from application menus. Adding the role without the keyboard model makes the control less predictable, so semantics should follow the interaction actually implemented.

sections.title: One open state across input methods
sections.content:
mouse click ─┐
touch tap ───┼→ toggle open state → aria-expanded + hidden → visible panel
Enter/Space ─┘
Escape → close → return focus to trigger

sections.title: Drive the panel from button state

followup_questions: When should a dropdown use ARIA menu roles?
What should happen to focus when the panel closes?
Why is :focus-within alone not enough for every dropdown?

questions.question: How would you diagnose and fix a janky CSS animation?
questions.title: Diagnosing a slow CSS animation
questions.direct_answer: Record the interaction in browser performance tools, identify long frames and repeated layout or paint work, then reduce the expensive work rather than guessing. Prefer transform or opacity for visual motion, limit the affected area, and retest on representative hardware.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can move from symptom to measured rendering cause.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding translateZ(0) or will-change everywhere without a trace.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe an evidence loop and include reduced-motion behaviour.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Reproduce the exact interaction and record a performance trace.
Look for long frames, layout, paint, and excessive layer work.
Replace unnecessary layout animation with transform or opacity.
Retest on target devices and with reduced motion enabled.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I first make the problem repeatable, disable unrelated activity, and record the interaction in the browser's Performance panel. The trace shows whether slow frames contain scripting, style calculation, layout, paint, or compositing work, which prevents a blind CSS rewrite.

If the animation changes width, height, top, or left every frame, I ask whether the visual result can use `transform` or `opacity` over a stable layout. I also check the size of painted areas, expensive shadows or filters, and whether many descendants change together.

For example, a sliding card animated with `left` may trigger layout and paint on each frame. Keeping its final layout fixed and animating `translateX` can move the rendered card without changing sibling geometry. The next trace should show whether that removed the measured work.

I treat `will-change` as a short, targeted hint, not a standard fix. Too many promoted layers consume memory and can increase compositing cost. I remove the hint when the effect is no longer imminent and verify actual layer behaviour in developer tools.

Finally, I test on a slower representative device, during real page load, and with `prefers-reduced-motion`. The animation is fixed only when the measured interaction is smooth and the reduced version preserves the same task and state feedback.

sections.title: Performance work is a measure-change-measure loop
sections.content: A dropped frame is an outcome, not a diagnosis. The trace identifies which rendering stage exceeds the available frame time. Change the smallest cause, record again, and keep the improvement only when the evidence changes.

sections.title: Layer promotion trades computation for memory
sections.content: Compositor-friendly properties can let the browser reuse painted content, but each separate layer has storage and management cost. A full-screen translucent layer or many animated cards can consume substantial memory. The browser decides promotion heuristically, so forcing every element with `will-change` may make the page worse. Reserve hints for known near-term animation and profile the complete scene.

sections.title: Debugging loop for dropped frames
sections.content: reproduce → record frames → locate script/style/layout/paint/composite cost → change one cause → record again → test target device

sections.title: Replace layout offsets with a visual transform

followup_questions: Which rendering stages appear in a browser performance trace?
Why should will-change be applied sparingly?
When must a layout property change despite its animation cost?

questions.question: Why can z-index fail to place an element above another one?
questions.title: Debugging z-index and stacking contexts
questions.direct_answer: z-index orders boxes within a stacking context; it cannot make a child escape above an element in a higher sibling context. Positioned elements with z-index and properties such as transform or opacity below 1 can create new stacking contexts, so the ancestors' order may decide the result.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner reasons about stacking-context hierarchy rather than choosing a larger integer.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Raising a descendant to z-index: 999999 while its parent remains in a lower context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace context creators upward and compare sibling contexts at their common parent.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: z-index is evaluated inside a stacking context.
A child cannot outrank a higher sibling context by using a huge number.
Positioned z-index, transforms, and opacity below 1 can create contexts.
Compare the nearest competing ancestor contexts, not only the leaf elements.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`z-index` is not one global number line for the whole page. Elements are painted inside stacking contexts, and each context participates as a single unit in its parent's stacking order. Descendants are sorted internally but cannot jump outside that unit.

Stacking contexts are created in several ways, including the root element, positioned elements with a non-auto z-index, fixed or sticky positioning in relevant cases, opacity below one, and a non-none transform. These properties can introduce a boundary even when layering was not their main purpose.

For example, a modal with z-index 10000 can remain under a header with z-index 2 if the modal is inside a transformed application wrapper whose entire context sits below the header's context. Increasing the modal's own number only changes its position inside the lower wrapper.

I inspect ancestors of both elements, identify where each stacking context begins, then compare the first sibling contexts that compete under a common parent. The fix may be moving the overlay to a top-level portal, removing an accidental context creator, or assigning intentional context levels to the ancestors.

I avoid arbitrary enormous values because they hide the hierarchy and make later overlays harder to place. A small documented scale for page chrome, popovers, and modals works when components are mounted in the intended context.

sections.title: Layering is a tree, not a flat scoreboard
sections.content: Each stacking context contains its own ordered children. When two leaves belong to different contexts, their leaf z-index values are never compared directly. The browser compares the ancestor contexts first and paints each as one atomic unit.

sections.title: Find the first common stacking parent
sections.content: Trace upward from each competing element and list every context creator. At the first parent context shared by both paths, compare the two immediate child contexts according to stacking rules. If the modal's branch loses there, no descendant value can repair it. Portaling overlays near the document root is common because it avoids component-local transforms and opacity contexts, but focus management and semantic ownership must still remain correct.

sections.title: Why a large child value can still lose
sections.content:
root stacking context
├─ app wrapper (z: 1, transform)
│  └─ modal (z: 10000)  ← trapped inside app unit
└─ header (z: 2)        ← entire unit paints above app

sections.title: Expose the ancestor that controls the result
